questions.q: A $72Ω$ galvanometer is shunted by a resistance of $8Ω$. The percentage of the total current which passes through the galvanometer is
questions.solution:
Let $G$ be resistance of galvanometer and $I '$ be the current passing through the galvanometer produces full scale deflection. If $I$ is the maximum current, and since, $G$ and $S$ are in parallel so, the potential difference between them will be same.

Then,

${I}^{'}G = {I}_{2}S ⇒ 72{I}^{'} = 8{I}_{2} ⇒ {I}_{2} = 9{I}^{'} ⇒ I = {I}^{'} + {I}_{2} = 10{I}^{'}$

So the percentage of total current passes through galvanometer is

$\dfrac{{I}^{'}}{I} \times 100$= \dfrac{{I}^{'}}{10{I}^{'}} \times 100 = 10 %$

questions.q: Two cells of the same EMF $E$ but different internal resistances ${r}_{1}$ and ${r}_{2}$ are connected in series with an external resistance $R$ as shown in the figure. The terminal potential difference across, the second cell is found to be zero. The external resistance $R$ must then be:

questions.q: A teacher in his physics laboratory allotted an experiment to determine the resistance $\left(G\right)$ a galvanometer. Students took the observations for $\dfrac{1}{3}$ deflection in the galvanometer. Which of the below is true for measuring value of $G$?

$\dfrac{1}{3}$ deflection method can be used and in this case, the G equals to three times the value of shunt resistance(s).

questions.solution:
If a large resistance $R$ is connected with a battery, then current will be approximately $\dfrac{ε}{R}$, and $t$ will remain almost constant.

In ${1}^{st}$ case, only $\left(G\right)$ is connected $⇒ ig = i$

In ${2}^{nd}$ case,

${i}_{g}{R}_{0} = \left(I - {i}_{g}\right)S ⇒ {\left({i}_{g}\right)}_{2} = \left(\dfrac{S}{{R}_{g} + S}\right)i$

If ${\left({i}_{g}\right)}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left({i}_{g}\right), ⇒ \left(\dfrac{S}{{R}_{g} + S}\right)i = \dfrac{1}{3}i$

${R}_{g} = 2S$

${R}_{g} = 2S$

questions.q: A potentiometer wire of length $10m$ and resistance $20Ω$ is connected in series with a $25V$ battery and an external resistance $30Ω$. A cell of emf $E$ in secondary circuit is balanced by $250cm$ long potentiometer wire. The value of $E$ (in volt) is $\dfrac{x}{10}$. The value of $x$ is _____ .
questions.solution:
Since the given resistance is in series, so, total resistance $\left(R\right) = 20 + 30 = 50Ω$

Given,

Potential difference$= 25V$

Current$\left(I\right) = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{25}{50} = 0 . 5A$

Also, Potential gradient $= \dfrac{{V}_{pd}}{L} = \dfrac{IR}{L}$

Where, ${V}_{pd} =$potential drop at wire

$L =$Length of wire

Potential gradient$= \dfrac{20 \times 0 .5}{10} = 1V{m}^{- 1}$

So, Emf of the cell is

$E =$Potential gradient$\times$Balancing Length

$E = 1 \times \dfrac{250}{100}$

$E = 2 . 5V = \dfrac{25}{10}V$

Thus, $x = 25$.

questions.q: Two identical cells each of emf $1 . 5V$ are connected in parallel across a parallel combination of two resistors each of resistance $20Ω$. A voltmeter connected in the circuit measures $1 . 2V$. The internal resistance of each cell is :
questions.solution:
Equivalent resistance of the parallel $20Ω$ branches will be $10Ω$.

Equivalent EMF of the two branches which are in parallel will be, $= \dfrac{\dfrac{1 . 5}{r} + \dfrac{1 . 5}{r}}{\dfrac{1}{r} + \dfrac{1}{r}} = 1 . 5V$ and the equivalent internal resistance for same branches will be, $\dfrac{r}{2}$.

For loop containing voltmeter and $10Ω$ resistor, $1 . 2 - 10i = 0 ⇒ i = 0 . 12A$.

Reading of voltmeter should be,

$1 . 2 = 1 . 5 - i\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right) ⇒ i\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right) = 0 . 3 ⇒ r = \dfrac{0 . 6}{i} = \dfrac{0 . 6}{0 . 12} = 5Ω$

questions.solution:
$R = \dfrac{ρℓ}{A} = \dfrac{V}{I}$
$ρ = \dfrac{AV}{Iℓ} = \dfrac{\pi{d}^{2}V}{4Iℓ}\left(A = \dfrac{\pi{d}^{2}}{4}\right)$
$∴ \dfrac{\Deltaρ}{ρ} = \dfrac{2\Deltad}{d} + \dfrac{\DeltaV}{V} + \dfrac{\DeltaI}{I} + \dfrac{\Deltaℓ}{ℓ}$
$\dfrac{\Deltaρ}{ρ} = 2\left(\dfrac{0 . 01}{5 . 00}\right) + \dfrac{0 . 1}{5 . 0} + \dfrac{0 . 01}{2 . 00} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{10 . 0}$
$\dfrac{\Deltaρ}{ρ} = 0 . 004 + 0 . 02 + 0 . 005 + 0 . 01$
$\dfrac{\Deltaρ}{ρ} = 0 . 039$
$%$ error $= \dfrac{\Deltaρ}{ρ} \times 100 = 0 . 039 \times 100 = 3 . 90 % .$

$= x = 6$

$= 125\pi \times {10}^{- 3}A$

Therefore, $i = 125\pimA$

Hence, $x = 5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A battery of $3.0\text{V}$ is connected to a resistor dissipating $0.5\text{W}$ of power. If the terminal voltage of the battery is $2.5\text{V}$, the power dissipated within the internal resistance is:
questions.solution:
Given,

Emf of the battery, $E = 3V$

Potential difference across resister $R$ is ${V}_{R} = 2 . 5V$

Power dissipation in the resister is $P = 0 . 5W$

By using Kirchhoff's voltage law is given by,

${V}_{r} + {V}_{R} = E . . . ( 1 )$

${V}_{r}$ is voltage across internal resister.

Using equation (1) and substitute the given values,

$⇒ {V}_{r} + 2 .5 = 3$

$⇒ {V}_{r} = 0 .5$

Now the ratio of potential across $R$ and $r$ is given by,

$\dfrac{{V}_{R}}{{V}_{r}} = \dfrac{IR}{Ir} = \dfrac{2 .5}{0 .5} = 5$

$⇒ \dfrac{R}{r} = 5$

Now the power dissipation across the internal resistance is given by

$\dfrac{{P}_{R}}{{P}_{r}} = \dfrac{{I}^{2}R}{{I}^{2}r} = \dfrac{R}{r}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{P}_{R}}{{P}_{r}} = 5$

$⇒ {P}_{r} = \dfrac{{P}_{R}}{5}$

$⇒ {P}_{r} = \dfrac{0 .5}{5} = 0 .1 W$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A moving coil galvanometer, having a resistance $G,$ produces full scale deflection when a current ${I}_{G}$ flows through it. This galvanometer can be converted into (i) an ammeter of range 0 to ${I}_{o}\left({I}_{0} > {I}_{g}\right)$ by connecting a shunt resistance ${R}_{A}$ to it and (ii) into a voltmeter of range 0 to $V\left(V = G{I}_{0}\right)$ by connecting a series resistance ${R}_{V}$ to it. Then,
questions.solution:
For ammeter: $\left({I}_{0} - {I}_{G}\right) \times {R}_{A} = {I}_{G} \times G ⇒ {I}_{0} = {I}_{G} \times \dfrac{\left(G + {R}_{A}\right)}{{R}_{A}}$
For voltmeter: ${V}_{0} = {I}_{G}\left(G + {R}_{V}\right)$
$∵ {V}_{0} = {I}_{0} \times G$
$⇒ {I}_{G} \times \left(G + {R}_{V}\right) = {I}_{G} \times \dfrac{\left(G + {R}_{A}\right) \times G}{{R}_{A}}$
$⇒ {R}_{A} \times G + {R}_{V} \times {R}_{A} = {G}^{2} + {R}_{A} \times G$
$⇒ {R}_{V}{R}_{A} = {G}^{2}$
Again, $\dfrac{{R}_{A}}{{R}_{V}} = \dfrac{{I}_{G} \times G}{{I}_{0} - {I}_{G}} \times \dfrac{{I}_{G}}{\left({I}_{0} - {I}_{G}\right) \times G} = \dfrac{{{I}_{G}}^{2}}{{\left({I}_{0} - {I}_{G}\right)}^{2}}$

questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance $100Ω$ has $50$ divisions on its scale and has sensitivity of $20\muA / division$ . It is to be converted to voltmeter with three ranges, of $0 - 2V, 0 - 10V$ and $0 - 20V .$ The appropriate circuit to do so is:
questions.solution:
Given, the resistance of the galvanometer $G = 100Ω$
No. of divisions $= 50$
Current Sensitivity $= 20\muA / division$

The maximum current through galvanometer will be
${I}_{max} = 50 \times 20 \times {10}^{- 6} = {10}^{- 3}A$
For ${V}_{1} = 2V$

using Ohm's law ${V}_{1} = {I}_{max}\left(G + {R}_{1}\right)$
$2 = {10}^{- 3} \times \left(100 + {R}_{1}\right)$
$∴ {R}_{1} = 1900Ω$

For ${V}_{2} = 10V$

using Ohm's law ${V}_{2} = {I}_{max}\left(G + {R}_{1} + {R}_{2}\right)$

$10 = {10}^{- 3} \times \left(100 + 1900 + {R}_{2}\right)$
$∴ {R}_{2} = 8000Ω$

For ${V}_{3} = 20V$

using Ohm's law ${V}_{3} = {I}_{max}\left(G + {R}_{1} + {R}_{2} + {R}_{3}\right)$
$20 = {10}^{- 3}\left(100 + 1900 + 8000 + {R}_{3}\right)$
$∴ {R}_{3} = 10 \times {10}^{3}Ω$

questions.q: Space between two concentric conducting spheres of radii $a$ and $b$( b > a )$ is filled with a medium of resistivity $ρ$ . The resistance between the two spheres will be:

Resistance of this volume along rational directions,

questions.q: A metal wire of resistance $3Ω$ is elongated to make a uniform wire of double its previous length. This new wire is now bent and the ends joined to make a circle. If two points on this circle make an angle ${60}^{o}$ at the center, the equivalent resistance between these two points will be:
questions.solution:
We know, $R = \dfrac{ρl}{A} = \dfrac{ρ{l}^{2}}{Al} = \dfrac{ρ{l}^{2}}{Volume}$
$R ∝ {l}^{2}$ , if the volume is constant.
$∴$ New resistance $= 4R$

${R}_{1} = \dfrac{4R}{360} \times 300 = \dfrac{10R}{3}$
${R}_{2} = \dfrac{4R}{360} \times 60 = \dfrac{2R}{3}$
$∴$ Equivalent resistance ${R}_{eq} = \dfrac{{R}_{1}{R}_{2}}{{R}_{1} + {R}_{2}}$
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{10R}{3} \times \dfrac{2R}{3}}{\dfrac{10R}{3} + \dfrac{2R}{3}} = \dfrac{5R}{9}$
$= \dfrac{5}{3}Ω$

questions.q: In a conductor, if the number of conduction electrons per unit volume is $8.5 \times {10}^{28}{m}^{- 3}$ and mean free time is $25fs$ (femto second), it’s approximate resistivity is: $\left({m}_{e} = 9.1 \times {10}^{- 31}kg\right)$
questions.solution:
We know $i = ne{Av}_{d}$
$⇒ i = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{VA}{ρl} = \dfrac{EA}{ρ}$
$ρ = \dfrac{EA}{i} = \dfrac{EA}{ne{Av}_{d}}$
Drift velocity can be written as ${v}_{d} = \dfrac{eE}{{m}_{e}}τ$
$ρ = \dfrac{EA{m}_{e}}{neAeEτ} = \dfrac{{m}_{e}}{n{e}^{2}τ}$
$= \dfrac{9.1 \times 1{0}^{- 31}}{8.5 \times 1{0}^{28} \times {\left(1.6 \times {10}^{- 19}\right)}^{2} \times 25 \times 1{0}^{- 15}}$
$\approx 1.65 \times 1{0}^{- 8}Ωm$

questions.q: A cell of internal resistance $r$ drives current through an external resistance $R .$ The power delivered by the cell to the external resistance will be maximum when:
questions.solution:
Current $i = \dfrac{E}{r + R}$
Power generated in $R$

$P = {i}^{2}R$
$P = \dfrac{{E}^{2}R}{( r + R{)}^{2}}$

for maximum power $\dfrac{dP}{dR} = 0$
${E}^{2}\left[\dfrac{( r + R{)}^{2} \times 1 - R \times 2 ( r + R )}{( r + R{)}^{4}}\right] = 0$
$⇒ \text{when,}r = R\text{then,}\dfrac{dP}{dR} = 0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two equal resistances when connected in series to a battery, consume electric power of $60 \mathrm{~W}$. If these resistance are now connected in parallel combination to the same battery, the electric power consumed will be :
questions.solution:
When two resistances are connected in series, $R_{e q}=2 R$

Power consumed, $\mathrm{P}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{ea}}}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2 \mathrm{R}}$

In parallel condition, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{R} / 2$ New power, $\mathrm{P}^{\prime}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{(\mathrm{R} / 2)}$

or $\mathrm{P}^{\prime}=4 \mathrm{P}=240 \mathrm{~W}(\because \mathrm{P}=60 \mathrm{~W})$

questions.q: The actual value of resistance $R$ , shown in the figure is $30Ω .$ This is measured in an experiment as shown using the standard formula $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ , where $V$ and $I$ are the readings of the voltmeter and ammeter, respectively. If the measured value of $R$ is $5%$ less, then the internal resistance of the voltmeter is:
questions.solution:
Measured value of $R = 5 %$ less than
actual value of $R$ i.e., ${R}^{'} = 30 - ( 5 %$ of $30$) = 30 - \dfrac{5}{100} \times 30$

${R}^{'} = 28 . 5Ω$. . . \left(i\right)$

Now, let us assume that internal resistance of voltmeter ${R}_{V}$. Replacing voltmeter with its internal resistance, we get following circuit.

It is clear that the measured value, ${R}^{'}$ should be equal to parallel combination of $R$ and ${R}_{V}$. Mathematically,
${R}^{'} = \dfrac{R \times {R}_{V}}{R + {R}_{V}} = 28 . 5Ω$

Given. $R = 30Ω$

$⇒ \dfrac{30{R}_{V}}{30 + {R}_{V}} = 28 . 5$

$⇒ 30{R}_{V} = \left(28 . 5 \times 30\right) + 28 . 5{R}_{V}$

$⇒ 1 . 5{R}_{V} = 28 . 5 \times 30$

$⇒ {R}_{V} = \dfrac{28 . 5 \times 30}{1 . 5} = 19 \times 30$

or ${R}_{V} = 570Ω$

questions.q: The Wheatstone bridge shown in the figure below, gets balanced when the carbon resistor used as ${R}_{1}$ has the colour code (orange, red, brown). The resistors ${R}_{2}$ and ${R}_{4}$ are $80Ω$ and $40Ω$, respectively. Assuming that the colour code for the carbon resistors gives their accurate values, the colour code for the carbon resistor, used as ${R}_{3}$, would be
questions.solution:
Colour band $A$ and $B$ indicate the first two significant figures of resistance in 'ohm', while the $C$ band gives the decimal multiplier i.e., the number of zeros that follows the two significant figures $A$ and $B$.

The last band $D$ indicates the tolerance in percentage about the indicated value or in other word, it represents the percentage accuracy of the indicated value.

For ${R}_{1}$, the given colour of the rings of a carbon resistor are orange, red, brown then, the value of resistance is

${R}_{1} = 32 \times {10}^{1}$

Condition for balance in the Wheat stone's bridge is

$\dfrac{{R}_{1}}{{R}_{3}} = \dfrac{{R}_{2}}{{R}_{4}}$

So, $\dfrac{320}{{R}_{3}} = \dfrac{80}{40}$

$∴ {R}_{3} = 160Ω$, so colour coding of resistor ${R}_{3}$ is

Brown$\to 1$

Blue$\to 6$

Brown$\to 1$
$16 \times {10}^{1} ⇒ 160Ω$

questions.q: In the given circuit the internal resistance of the $18V$ cell is negligible. If ${R}_{1} = 400Ω, {R}_{3} = 100Ω$ and ${R}_{4} = 500Ω$ and the reading of an ideal voltmeter across ${R}_{4}$ is $5V,$ then the value of ${R}_{2}$ will be:
questions.solution:
Given reading of an ideal voltmeter for resistance ${R}_{4}$ is ${V}_{4} = 5V$, then current (let ${i}_{1}$)is given branch (as resistance ${R}_{3}$ in series with resistance ${R}_{4}$) is
${i}_{1} = \dfrac{V}{{R}_{4}} = \dfrac{5}{500} = 0 . 01A$
Then for resistance ${R}_{3}$, the potential difference will be

${V}_{3} = {i}_{1}{R}_{3} = 0 . 01 \times 100 = 1V$

So, for given branch of resistance potential difference is

${V}_{3} + {V}_{4} = 1 + 5 = 6V$

From figure for resistance ${R}_{1}, {R}_{3}$ and ${R}_{4}$ a total applied potential difference is $18V$ then,

${V}_{1} + {V}_{3} + {V}_{4} = 18 ∴ {V}_{1} = 18 - \left({V}_{3} + {V}_{4}\right) = 18 - 6 = 12V$

So, the total current drawn from the source is

$∴$ Current through ${R}_{2}$

${i}_{2} = 0 \cdot 03 - 0 \cdot 01 = 0 \cdot 02A$
and potential difference for ${R}_{2}$ is

${V}_{2} = {V}_{3} + {V}_{4} = 6V$ ( ${R}_{2}$ is in parallel arrangement with the resistances ${R}_{3}$ and ${R}_{4}$)

Now the value of resistance ${R}_{2}$ is :
${V}_{2} = {i}_{2}{R}_{2} ⇒ {R}_{2} = \dfrac{{V}_{2}}{{i}_{2}} = \dfrac{6}{0 \cdot 02} = 300Ω$

questions.q: Mobility of electrons in a semiconductor is defined as the ratio of their drift velocity to the applied electric field. If, for an $\text{N}$-type semiconductor, the density of electrons is ${10}^{19}m^{- 3}$ and their mobility is $1.6m^{2}V^{- 1}s^{- 1}$, then the resistivity of the semiconductor (since it is an $\text{N}$-type semiconductor contribution of holes is ignored) is close to:
questions.solution:
Resistivity $ρ = \dfrac{E}{J} = \dfrac{E}{ne{υ}_{d}} = \dfrac{1}{ne\mu}$

$\mu =$ mobility

$ρ = \dfrac{1}{{10}^{19} \times 1.6 \times {10}^{- 19} \times 1.6} = \dfrac{1}{2.56}Ωm$

$= 0.4Ωm$

questions.solution:
We are given a galvanometer connected in the first circuit in the above figure, where $E = 6V$, $R = 11kΩ$ and the deflection $\theta = 9$ divisions. The galvanometer has a resistance of $G$. The current in the circuit,

$I = \dfrac{E}{R + G} . . . ( 1 )$

Also, since the figure of merit is $60\mu A / division$

$I = 60 \times 9\mu A = 540\mu A . . . ( 2 )$

Substituting equation $( 2 )$ in $( 1 )$,

$540 \times {10}^{- 6} = \dfrac{6}{11, 000 + G} ⇒ G = \dfrac{6}{540 \times {10}^{- 6}} - 11, 000 ⇒ G = 111Ω . . . ( 3 )$

In the second circuit, it is given that the deflection is half that of the previous circuit. So, current flowing through the galvanometer half the first circuit. Hence,

$⇒ S = \dfrac{RG \times \dfrac{I}{2}}{E - \dfrac{( R + G ) I}{2}}$

$S = \dfrac{11 \times {10}^{3} \times 111 \times \dfrac{540}{2} \times {10}^{- 6}}{6 - \left(\dfrac{6}{2}\right)} = 110Ω$

questions.solution:
As shown in figure two cells are connected in parallel with the load resistance of $R = 10Ω$. Let current ${i}_{1}, {i}_{2}$ drawn from both cells as shown, from $K . C . L . i = {i}_{1} + {i}_{2} . . . \left(1\right)

Apply $K . V . L .$ for loop $ACDF$,

${E}_{1} - iR - {i}_{1}{r}_{1} = 0 ⇒ 12 - 10i - {i}_{1} = 0 . . . $\left(2\right)$

From equations $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(2\right)$

$12 - 11{i}_{1} - 10{i}_{2} = 0 . . . \left(3\right)

Now,$ for loopBCDE$,

Apply $K . V . L .

${E}_{2} - 10i - {i}_{2}{r}_{2} = 0 ⇒ 13 - 10i - 2{i}_{2} = 0 ⇒ \left(∵ i = {i}_{1} + {i}_{2}\right)$ ∴ 13 - 10{i}_{1} - 12{i}_{2} = 0 . . . $\left(4\right)$

From equation $\left(3\right)$ and $\left(4\right)$,

${i}_{1} = \dfrac{7}{16}A,$ {i}_{2} = $\dfrac{23}{32}A$

So, net current in external load $R = 10Ω$ is

$\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S} . . . \left(1\right)

$\dfrac{4}{60} = \dfrac{Q}{40}$

$⇒ Q = \dfrac{16}{6} = \dfrac{8}{3}Ω$

Now, $P = ρl = 80l$

and $Q = ρ\left(100 - l\right)Q = ρ\left(100 - 80\right) = 20ρ$

$\dfrac{4 + R}{80} = \dfrac{Q}{20} ⇒ \dfrac{4 + R}{80} = \dfrac{\dfrac{8}{3}}{20}\left(∵ Q = \dfrac{8}{3}\right) ⇒ \dfrac{4 + R}{80} = \dfrac{8}{60} ⇒ R = \dfrac{20}{3}Ω$

In the given infinite network problems, let, $X$ be an equivalent resistance. If we connect one section of an infinite network with the replacing network using an equivalent resistance, then in this new equivalent circuit the equivalent resistance will still remain the same.

$x = \dfrac{8 + 6x}{4 + x}$

where, $V = 9Volt, r = 0 \cdot 5Ω, R = 4Ω$.

Then, from the above equation,

$I = \dfrac{9}{4 + 0 .5} = 2A$.

Power in “r”

$P = {I}_{2}^{2} r = {[ I \times \dfrac{R}{R + r} ]}^{2} r = {I}^{2} \dfrac{{R}^{2} r}{{( R + r )}^{2}}$

$P = {[ \dfrac{E}{R + \dfrac{R \times fR}{R + fR}} ]}^{2} \dfrac{{R}^{2} ( fR )}{{( R + fR )}^{2}} = \dfrac{{E}^{2} {R}^{2} fR}{{R}^{2} {[ 1 + \dfrac{f}{( f + 1 )} ]}^{2} {R}^{2} {( 1 + f )}^{2}}$

$P = \dfrac{{E}^{2} f}{R{( 1 + 2f )}^{2}}$

For $P( max )\dfrac{dP}{df} = 0$

$\dfrac{{E}^{2}}{R} = [ \dfrac{{( 1 + 2f )}^{2} - f{ 2( 1 + 2f )( 0 + 2 ) }}{{( 1 + 2f )}^{2}} ] = 0$

${( 1 + 2f )}^{2} = 4f( 1 + 2f )$

$1 + 2f = 4f$

$f = \dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.q: To know the resistance $G$ of a galvanometer by half deflection method, a battery of emf ${V}_{E}$ and resistance $R$ is used to deflect the galvanometer by angle $\theta$ . If a shunt of resistance $S$ is needed to get half deflection the $G$, $R$ and $S$ are related by the equation:
questions.solution:
Let resistance $S$ is connected with galvanometer of resistance $G$, than

${I}_{G} = \dfrac{V}{R + G}$


Now, as shown below figure a shunt $S$ is connected in parallel with the galvanometer for half deflection in it, that is ${I}_{G} ' = \dfrac{{I}_{G}}{2}$, than

$I = \dfrac{V}{R + \dfrac{GS}{G + S}}$


As, shunt and galvanometer are in parallel then ${V}_{G} = {V}_{S}$
${I}_{G} ' G = \left(I - {I}_{G} '\right)S$

$⇒ {I}_{G} ' \left(G + S\right) = IS$
$⇒ \dfrac{{I}_{G}}{2} = \dfrac{IS}{G + S}\left(∵ {I}_{G} ' = \dfrac{{I}_{G}}{2}\right)$

On, substituting the values of ${I}_{G}$ and $I$ in above equation

$\dfrac{V}{2\left(R + G\right)} = \dfrac{V}{R + \dfrac{GS}{G + S}} \times \dfrac{S}{G + S}$
$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2\left(R + G\right)} = \dfrac{S}{R\left(G + S\right) + GS}$
$⇒ R\left(G + S\right) + GS = 2S\left(R + G\right)$
$⇒ RG + RS + GS = 2S\left(R + G\right)$
$⇒ RG = 2S\left(R + G\right) - S\left(R + G\right)$
$⇒ RG = S\left(R + G\right)$

questions.q: A $50Ω$ resistance is connected to a battery of $5V$. A galvanometer of resistance $100Ω$ is to be used as an ammeter to measure current through the resistance, for this a resistance ${r}_{S}$ is connected to the galvanometer. Which of the following connections should be employed if the measured current is with in $1 %$ of the current without the ammeter in the circuit?
questions.solution:
Initially current in the circuit is

$I = \dfrac{5}{50} = 0.1$

and the current in circuit when ammeter is connected,is $1 %$ of initial current , i.e., ${I}^{′} = \dfrac{1}{100} \times 0 \cdot 1 = 0.099A$

To increase the range of galvanometer, let resistance ${r}_{s}$
is connected parallel to it and along with $50Ω$ is connected in series to ammeter. So, equivalent resistance of circuit is:

${R}_{eq} = 50 + \dfrac{100{r}_{S}}{100 + {r}_{S}}$

Now, From equation $V = {I}^{'}{R}_{eq}$

$5 = 0 . 099 \times \left(50 + \dfrac{100{r}_{s}}{100 + {r}_{s}}\right) ⇒ 50 + \dfrac{100{r}_{s}}{100 + {r}_{s}} = \dfrac{5}{0 . 099} ⇒ 50 + \dfrac{100{r}_{s}}{100 + {r}_{s}} = 50 . 5050 ⇒ \dfrac{100{r}_{s}}{100 + {r}_{s}} = 50 . 5050 ⇒ {r}_{s} = 0 . 5Ω$

Potential difference$= 5V$, length $= \text{0.1 m} = l$ and the electron speed $=$ drift velocity ${\text{v}}_{\text{d}} = \text{2.5} \times 1{0}^{- 4}{\text{m s}}^{- 1}$, electron density $\left(\text{n}\right) = 8 \times 1 {0}^{2 8} {\text{m}}^{- 3}$ and the charge on each electron(e) $= \text{1.6} \times 1{0}^{- 19}\text{C}$. $ρ = \dfrac{\text{AR}}{l}$\left[ρ = \text{Resistivity}\right]$

$= \dfrac{\text{A}}{l} \times \dfrac{V}{\text{i}}$ [from (ii)]$= \dfrac{\text{Av}}{l \times \text{nA}\text{e}{\text{v}}_{\text{d}}}$ & [from (i)]$= \dfrac{\text{V}}{l \times \text{n} \times \text{e} \times {\text{v}}_{\text{d}}}$

questions.question: When $5V$ potential difference is applied across a wire of length $0 . 1m$, the drift speed of electrons is $2.5 \times {10}^{- 4}m{s}^{- 1}$ . If the electron density in the wire is $8 \times {10}^{28}{m}^{- 3}$ , the resistivity of the material is close to:

Potential difference$= 5V$, length $= \text{0.1 m} = l$ and the electron speed $=$ drift velocity ${\text{v}}_{\text{d}} = \text{2.5} \times 1{0}^{- 4}{\text{m s}}^{- 1}$, electron density $\left(\text{n}\right) = 8 \times 1 {0}^{2 8} {\text{m}}^{- 3}$ and the charge on each electron(e) $= \text{1.6} \times 1{0}^{- 19}\text{C}$. Resistance $R$ is also equal to, $\dfrac{ρl}{\text{A}}$\text{⇒}\text{R} = \dfrac{ρl}{\text{A}}$

$ρ = \dfrac{\text{AR}}{l}$\left[ρ = \text{Resistivity}\right]$

$= \dfrac{\text{A}}{l} \times \dfrac{V}{\text{i}}$ [from (ii)]$= \dfrac{\text{Av}}{l \times \text{nA}\text{e}{\text{v}}_{\text{d}}}$ & [from (i)]$= \dfrac{\text{V}}{l \times \text{n} \times \text{e} \times {\text{v}}_{\text{d}}}$

$= \dfrac{5}{\text{0.1} \times 8 \times 1 {0}^{2 8} \times \text{1.6} \times 1 {0}^{- 1 9} \times \text{2.5} \times 1 {0}^{- 4}}$

$= \text{0.156} \times 1{0}^{- 4}Ω\text{m} = \text{1.56} \times 1{0}^{- 5}Ω\text{m}$

questions.q: The supply voltage to a room is $120 V$. The resistance of the lead wires is $6 Ω$. A $60 W$ bulb is already switched on. What is the decrease of voltage across the bulb, when a $240 W$ heater is switched on in parallel to the bulb?
questions.solution:
Resistance of bulb, ${R}_{b} = \dfrac{{V}^{2}}{{P}_{b}} = \dfrac{120 \times 120}{60} = 240Ω$
Resistance of heater, ${R}_{h} = \dfrac{{V}^{2}}{{P}_{h}} = \dfrac{120 \times 120}{240} = 60Ω$

Voltage across bulb before the heater is not connected, ${V}_{1} = \dfrac{V \times {R}_{b}}{{R}_{b} + 6} = \dfrac{120 \times 240V}{246} = 117 . 07V$

Now the bulb and heater are connected in parallel.

Resistance of the combination is ${R}_{net} = \dfrac{240 \times 60}{240 + 60} = 48Ω$
Voltage across bulb after the heater is switched on,
${V}_{2} = \dfrac{V \times {R}_{net}}{{R}_{net} + 6} = \dfrac{120 \times 48}{48 + 6} = 106 . 66V$

The decrease in the voltage is ${V}_{1} - {V}_{2} = 117 . 07 - 106 . 66 ≃ 10 . 4V$

Note: Here supply voltage is taken as rated voltage.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an experiment of potentiometer for measuring the internal resistance of primary cell a balancing length $\ell$ is obtained on the potentiometer wire when the cell is open circuit. Now the cell is short circuited by a resistance $R$. If $R$ is to be equal to the internal resistance of the cell the balancing length on the potentiometer wire will be
questions.solution:
Balancing length $l$ will give emf of cell $\therefore E=K l$
Here $\mathrm{K}$ is potential gradient.
If the cell is short circuited by resistance 'R'
Let balancing length obtained be $l^{\prime}$ then

$\begin{aligned}$& V=k l^{\prime} \\
& r=$\left(\frac{E-V}{V}\right)$R \\
\Rightarrow & V=E-V \\
\Rightarrow & 2 V=E \\
$\text{ or, }$& 2 K l^{\prime}=K l \\
\therefore \quad & l^{\prime}=$\frac{l}{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A $6.0$ volt battery is connected to two light bulbs as shown in figure. Light bulb 1 has resistance 3 ohm while light bulb 2 has resistance $6 \mathrm{ohm}$. Battery has negligible internal resistance. Which bulb will glow brighter?
options:
Bulb 1 will glow more first and then its brightness will become less than bulb 2

Bulb 1

Bulb 2

Both glow equally
questions.solution:
Total resistance $=\frac{6 \times 3}{6+3}=2 \Omega$ Current in circuit $=\frac{6}{2}=3 A$
Therefore current through bulb 1 is $2 \mathrm{~A}$ and bulb 2 is $1 A$. So bulb 1 will glow more.

questions.q: Three resistors of $4 \Omega, 6 \Omega$ and $12 \Omega$ are connected in parallel and the combination is connected in series with a $1.5 \mathrm{~V}$ battery of $1 \Omega$ internal resistance. The rate of Joule heating in the $4 \Omega$ resistor is
questions.solution:
Resistors $4 \Omega, 6 \Omega$ and $12 \Omega$ are connected in parallel, its equivalent resistance $(R)$ is given by

$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{12} \Rightarrow$R=$\frac{12}{6}=$2 \Omega

Again $R$ is connected to $1.5 \mathrm{~V}$ battery whose internal resistance $r=1 \Omega$.
Equivalent resistance now,

R^{\prime}=2 \Omega+1 \Omega=3 \Omega

Current, $I_{\text{total }}=\frac{V}{R^{\prime}}=\frac{1.5}{3}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~A}\begin{aligned}$& I_${\text{total }}$=$\frac{1}{2}=$3 x+2 x+x=6 x \\
& \Rightarrow x=$\frac{1}{12}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Current through $4 \Omega$ resistor $=3 x$
=3 $\times \frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{~A}$Therefore, rate of Joule heating in the $4 \Omega$ resistor

=I² R=$\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^$2 $\times$4=$\frac{1}{4}=$0.25 $\mathrm{~W}$

questions.q:
Two electric bulbs marked $25 \mathrm{~W}-220 \mathrm{~V}$ and $100 \mathrm{~W}-220 \mathrm{~V}$ are connected in series to a $440 \mathrm{~V}$ supply. 
Which of the bulbs will fuse?
questions.solution:
Resistances of both the bulbs are
$\mathrm{R}_1=\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{P}_1}=\frac{220^2}{25}$\mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{P}_2}=\frac{220^2}{100}$
Hence $R_1>R_2$
When connected in series, the voltages divide in them in the ratio of their resistances. The voltage of $440\mathrm{~V}$ devides in such a way that voltage across $25 \mathrm{~w}$ bulb will be more than $220 \mathrm{~V}$.
Hence $25 \mathrm{~w}$ bulb will fuse.

Paragraph: Consider a block of conducting material of resistivity ' $\rho$ ' shown in the figure. Current 'l' enters at 'A' and leaves from ' $\mathrm{D}$ '. We apply superposition principle to find voltage ' $\Delta \mathrm{V}$ ' developed between ' $\mathrm{B}$ ' and ' $\mathrm{C}$ '. The calculation is done in the following steps: (i) Take current 'l' entering from 'A' and assume it to spread over a hemispherical surface in the block. (ii) Calculate field $E(r)$ at distance ' $r$ ' from $A$ by using Ohm's law $E=\rho j$, where $j$ is the current per unit area at ' $r$ '. (iii) From the ' $r$ ' dependence of $E(r)$, obtain the potential $V(r)$ at $r$. (iv) Repeat (i), (ii) and (iii) for current 'l' leaving ' $D$ ' and superpose results for ' $A$ ' and ' $D$ '.
Question: $\Delta \mathrm{V}$ measured between $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{C}$ is
options:
$\frac{\rho l}{\pi a}-\frac{\rho l}{\pi(a+b)}$

$\frac{\rho l}{a}-\frac{\rho l}{(a+b)}$

$\frac{\rho l}{2 \pi a}-\frac{\rho l}{2 \pi(a+b)}$

$\frac{\rho l}{2 \pi(a-b)}$
questions.solution:
Choosing $A$ as origin,
$
\begin{gathered}
E=\rho j=\rho \frac{1}{2 \pi r^2} \\
V_C-V_B=-\frac{\rho l}{2 \pi} \int_a^{(a+b)} \frac{1}{r^2} d r=\frac{\rho l}{2 \pi}\left[\frac{1}{(a+b)}-\frac{1}{a}\right] \\
V_B-V_C=\frac{\rho l}{2 \pi}\left[\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{(a+b)}\right]
\end{gathered}
$

questions.q: The resistance of the series combination of two resistances is $S$. When they are joined in parallel through total resistance is $P$. If $S=n P$, then the minimum possible value of $n$ is
questions.question: The resistance of the series combination of two resistances is $S$. When they are joined in parallel through total resistance is $P$. If $S=n P$, then the minimum possible value of $n$ is
questions.explanation:
Let resistances be $R_1$ and $R_2$
So, $S=R_1+R_2$;
$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}=\frac{\mathrm{R}_1 \mathrm{R}_2}{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2} \\
& \mathrm{~S}=\mathrm{nP} \\
& \mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{nR}_1 \mathrm{R}_2}{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2} \\
& \left(\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2\right)^2=\mathrm{nR}_1 \mathrm{R}_2
\end{aligned}
$
If $R_1=R_2$, so minimum value of $n=4$.

questions.q: In a metre bridge experiment null point is obtained at $20 \mathrm{~cm}$ from one end of the wire when resistance $X$ is balanced against another resistance $Y$. If $X < Y$, then where will be the new position of the null point from the same end, if one decides to balance a resistance of $4 X$ against Y?
questions.solution: We have from meter bridge experiment, $\frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}$, where $\ell_2=\left(100-\ell_1\right) \mathrm{cm}$ In the first case, $X / Y=20 / 80$ In the second case $\frac{4 X}{Y}=\frac{\ell}{100-\ell}$\ell=50 \mathrm{~cm}$.
